cards.explanation: The catch is that he did it, but not wholeheartedly. The text says he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, “…but not wholeheartedly.” It's like me stamping a whole tray while my mind drifts off to the cooling rack. The cookies look fine, but my heart's not in the dough. I think a verdict like that is worth sitting with, friends.

The man of God tells him not to let the troops go with him, friends. He says, “O king, do not let the army of Israel go with you…” That's a hard thing to hear right after you've paid for an army. But the message is plain, and it's about those troops staying home.

The reason is that the LORD is not with Israel, friends. The man of God says, “…the LORD is not with Israel—not with any of the Ephraimites.” The reason he gives isn't about the soldiers' skill. It's about the LORD not being with Israel.

He brings home the gods of Edom, friends. The text says he brought back the gods of the Seirites. Seir is the land of the men he fought. He came back with idols, and that's where the trouble starts.

The point is that those gods couldn't deliver their own people from him, friends. The prophet asks, “Why have you sought this people’s gods, which could not deliver them from your hand?” Those gods didn't rescue the people who served them. The question is why Amaziah would turn to them anyway.

The prophet stops, but he gives one last word, friends. The text says he stopped, but he said, “I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not heeded my advice.” He quits talking, but he still gets that last word in. I think that takes some nerve.
